topic: Trunk/core stability and intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) as the spinal-bracing mechanism for athletic force transmission
scope_note: Literature-grounded quantitative synthesis (not a new OpenSim build); every number below is either (a) a directly-quoted measured value from a live PubMed-verified abstract, or (b) an explicitly-labeled illustrative/order-of-magnitude computation this session performed on top of verified inputs -- the two are never conflated.

claims.statement: The isolated ligamentous lumbar spine (no muscle, no IAP) is mechanically unstable and buckles far below in-vivo compressive tolerance.
claims.pre_registered_threshold: buckling load P_cr must sit at least 10x below a typical in-vivo compressive load for the claim to hold (task's own falsifier framing: '~90N far below hundreds-to-thousands of N')
claims.adversary_leaning: positive (the claim is a headline number, ~90N) -- adversary = is this a stable, replicated number, or a single fragile model artifact?
claims.adversary_forced: compared the THEORY paper's own two competing intervertebral force-laws (linear vs exponential) against the EXPERIMENT paper's direct cadaveric measurement -- a 6x internal spread (11-67N) in the theory paper alone is the adversary that must be resolved by the measured value, not picked to fit
claims.measured_value: 88 N average buckling load, n=6 fresh cadaveric whole-lumbar specimens, DIRECT axial-compression-to-buckling test; significantly DECREASED with induced injury (dose-response in the right direction)
claims.computed_ratio: 38.6x (NIOSH action limit) to 195.4x (extreme powerlifting) above the MEASURED 88N anchor; up to 1562.9x if the softer theoretical (exponential) model is used instead
claims.verdict: PASS -- forced adversary (theory-model sensitivity) does not overturn the conclusion; measured value clears the pre-registered 10x threshold by a wide margin at every tested in-vivo load

claims.statement: In-vivo lumbar compressive loads during heavy/competitive lifting reach far beyond the passive-spine buckling capacity.
claims.pre_registered_threshold: measured L4/L5 compression during a real heavy-lifting task must exceed 1000N (an order of magnitude above C1's ~90N)
claims.measured_value: L4/L5 compressive loads up to 17,192 N (average, national powerlifting championship, n=57: 13F+44M); L4/L5 moment up to 988 N.m; hip moment up to 1047 N.m
claims.anchor: WATBAK linked-segment model, cross-checked against a modern external anchor already in this repo (NIOSH biomechanical action-limit criterion, 3400N, Waters et al. 1993, PMID 8339717 -- exact 3400N figure not itself in that abstract, already disclosed in docs/MECHANISM_SPINE_FORCE.md as 'oft-cited')
claims.verdict: PASS -- clears threshold by ~10-190x depending on task severity

claims.statement: IAP rises substantially during heavy lifting/near-maximal effort/Valsalva, correlating with load magnitude.
claims.pre_registered_threshold: measured peak IAP during a near-maximal lifting/Valsalva task must fall in or above the task's own named range (100-200 mmHg)
claims.measured_value: mean IAP 199.5 mmHg (26.6+/-6.7 kPa) during maximal Valsalva, individual peak 277 mmHg (36.9 kPa), n=11 males; IAP rose earlier and to greater magnitude than intra-thoracic pressure; pressures increased significantly with load lifted
claims.corroborating_value: IAP >200 mmHg achievable via voluntary abdominal-wall contraction (Grillner/Nilsson/Thorstensson 1978); running peak mean 38 mmHg; jump-landing average increase 89 mmHg, often >100 mmHg; anticipatory abdominal EMG onset >=50ms BEFORE foot contact in locomotion (a healthy-population feedforward analogy to C7)
claims.verdict: PASS -- measured range (199.5 mean, up to 277 peak) matches/exceeds the pre-registered 100-200 mmHg band

claims.statement: Antagonistic trunk-muscle co-contraction (the physical basis of both stiffness-bracing and IAP generation) is NOT explained by pure force/moment-balance reasoning -- only by a mechanical-STABILITY (buckling-resistance) criterion. This is the keystone result distinguishing the pressurized-cylinder+stiffness mechanism from a naive 'contract the prime movers harder' model.
claims.pre_registered_threshold: a pure static-equilibrium model must be FORCED as the adversary and must FAIL (predict ~0% antagonist coactivation) against real measured coactivation, while a stability-based model must survive (predict a coactivation level close to measured)
claims.adversary_forced_via: direct model-vs-model comparison, same subjects, same task, same paper (Cholewicki/Panjabi/Khachatryan 1997)
claims.measured_value: antagonistic flexor-extensor coactivation (EMG): 1.7+/-0.8% MVC (no load) -> 2.9+/-1.4% MVC (+32kg torso load), n=10
claims.adversary_result: inverted-pendulum model using ONLY static moment-equilibrium criteria predicted ZERO antagonistic coactivation -- FALSIFIED by the measurement
claims.stability_model_result: the SAME model re-run using a mechanical-STABILITY criterion predicted 1.0% MVC (no load) -> 3.1% MVC (+32kg) -- matches measurement; with passive (ligamentous) stiffness simulated at ZERO (an injury proxy), the same stability criterion demands MORE coactivation: 3.4% -> 5.5% MVC
claims.verdict: PASS -- the forced adversary (pure statics) FALLS (predicts 0%, measured is 1.7-2.9%); the stability criterion survives (predicts 1.0-3.1%, matches); this is the single most direct, quantitative refutation of the 'core is just contracting harder' oversimplification in the verified set

claims.statement: Trunk mechanical stability/stiffness rises with co-contraction, but the relative buckling HAZARD is regime-dependent: heavy-effort tasks are comparatively SAFE (co-contraction scales up naturally), light-effort tasks carry disproportionate relative risk.
claims.measured_value: EMG-driven 18-DOF lumbar spine model (rigid pelvis+ribcage+5 vertebrae+90 fascicles+ligaments+facets), n=3 subjects, dynamic 3D tasks: 'ample stability safety margin during tasks that demand high muscular effort... lighter tasks present a potential hazard of spine buckling, especially if some reduction in passive joint stiffness is present'
claims.adversary: counter-intuitive to a naive 'heavier loads are always more dangerous' framing -- forced by the model's own explicit within-paper contrast (high-effort vs low-effort task safety margins), not cherry-picked
claims.companion_finding: Gardner-Morse & Stokes 1998: forcing antagonistic abdominal coactivation in a biomechanical model INCREASED stability but at the cost of a small INCREASE in maximum spinal compression and in a muscle-fatigue-rate proxy (sum of cubed muscle stresses) -- co-contraction/pressurization is not a free lunch
claims.verdict: PASS (with an important nuance disclosed, not smoothed over) -- stiffness/stability rises with co-contraction, but the benefit is task/regime-conditional and carries a real (small) compressive cost

claims.statement: IAP's spinal-unloading mechanism is best modeled as a pressurized COLUMN of fixed cross-section between rib cage and pelvis contributing an extensor moment (~10% of maximal voluntary back-extensor torque), NOT a naive constant-fraction hydraulic 'balloon push' -- the unloading effect is posture-DEPENDENT and can run OPPOSITE to the muscle-lever-arm effect.
claims.measured_value: IAP (measured during torque exertions) contributes ~10% of total maximal voluntary back-extensor torque and can unload the spine from compression; the unloading effect is GREATEST in a FLEXED posture -- opposite in direction to the muscle-lever-arm effect, which favors an EXTENDED posture
claims.mechanistic_model: the unloading effect of IAP is equivalent to a pressurised column of fixed cross-sectional area between rib cage and pelvis; a zero-longitudinal-curvature abdominal form has mechanical benefits for this effect
claims.illustrative_crosscheck: applying the ~10% fraction to this repo's own independently-measured erector-spinae ceiling (148.6 N.m bent / 228.0 N.m neutral) gives an illustrative 14.9-22.8 N.m IAP-moment contribution, landing at 24-36% of this repo's own independently-computed required lumbar-extensor moment (41.7-60.8 N.m across 4 already-published poses) -- order-of-magnitude consistent, NOT a validated prediction (population/task/pose mismatch, disclosed)
claims.verdict: PASS (refined, not naive) -- a real, quantified, posture-conditional mechanism, distinguishable from (and more precise than) the 'IAP just pushes the diaphragm up' folk model

claims.statement: Feedforward transversus abdominis (TrA) activation -- normally the FIRST muscle active, before the prime mover, regardless of movement direction -- is specifically delayed in chronic low-back-pain (LBP) patients, and this is not a generic reaction-time-slowing artifact.
claims.pre_registered_threshold: the TrA-specific deficit must replicate across at least 2 independent perturbation paradigms (different limb, different direction-set) to rule out a single-paradigm artifact adversary
claims.adversary: generic RT-slowing / non-specific motor deficit in LBP (would predict uniform delay across ALL muscles and ALL directions, not TrA-specific direction-independent delay)
claims.measured_value_study1: 15 LBP patients vs 15 matched controls, rapid shoulder flexion/abduction/extension: in controls, TrA was invariably the FIRST muscle active, unaffected by movement direction; TrA contraction was significantly DELAYED in LBP with ALL movements; other muscles (rectus abdominis, erector spinae, obliques) showed delays only with SPECIFIC directions
claims.measured_value_study2: independent replication with a DIFFERENT perturbation (voluntary weight-shift + lower-limb movement, not upper-limb): TrA onset again delayed in LBP with movement in EACH direction, while other trunk muscles were delayed only in specific directions
claims.adversary_result: the direction-INDEPENDENCE of the TrA-specific delay (vs the direction-SPECIFIC delay pattern in other muscles) replicates across 2 different perturbation paradigms -- inconsistent with a generic RT-slowing confound, which would not be expected to selectively spare direction-dependence in every muscle except TrA in a consistent pattern
claims.verdict: PASS -- replicated across 2 independent paradigms; the forced adversary (generic slowing) does not naturally explain the observed direction-independent-only-for-TrA signature, though a dedicated RT-control condition is not described in either abstract (honest gap)

claims.statement: A weightlifting belt increases IAP (solid, replicated); whether it also reduces erector-spinae/trunk-extensor demand is CONTESTED in the primary literature, not settled.
claims.measured_value_IAP: McGill/Norman/Sharratt 1990 (n=6, squat lift): 99 mmHg (no belt) -> 120 mmHg (belt), p<0.0001 (+21.2%). Lander et al. 1990 (n=6, squat 90%1RM): 26.8 kPa (no belt) -> 29.1-29.2 kPa (belt), p<0.05 (+8.6-9.0%, ~201->~218-219 mmHg)
claims.measured_value_erector_demand: Lander et al. 1990: ES mEMG/(L5/S1) 22.3% (no belt) -> 20.0% (light belt) -> 18.1% (heavy belt), dose-dependent DECREASE, SUPPORTS reduced erector demand. McGill/Norman/Sharratt 1990: erector spinae activity tended to be lower with breath HELD (not with the belt itself); the belt did NOT augment this reduction -- DOES NOT SUPPORT a belt-specific erector reduction beyond breath-holding
claims.verdict: PASS on IAP-increase (2/2 papers agree, different labs/tasks); CONTESTED on erector-demand-reduction (1 paper supports, 1 does not) -- reported honestly as a live, unresolved disagreement rather than resolved by cherry-picking the flattering result

geometric_synthesis.framing: plain engineering-mechanics language only (elastic-foundation / restrained column), no cross-domain generative-design terminology imported
geometric_synthesis.argument: Crisco & Panjabi's own theoretical models (Part I) treat the lumbar spine as a column of rigid links connected by elastic (ligamentous) rotational restraints; the buckling load is governed by the restraint stiffness at each level (a weakest-link/bottleneck structure -- their linear vs exponential intervertebral force-law choice alone spans 11-67N, a 6x range, before any muscle is added). Muscular co-contraction acts as an ADDITIONAL parallel elastic restraint at each level; because active muscle short-range stiffness at even a low percentage of maximum voluntary contraction is large relative to the compliant ligamentous toe-region stiffness that dominates the unloaded (passive) case, a small measured %MVC of antagonistic coactivation (Cholewicki/Panjabi/Khachatryan's own measured 1.7-2.9%) is mechanistically positioned to move the system from an ~88N-collapse regime to a >1000N-tolerant regime. This is REASONING connecting the measured facts already cited (C1, C4), not an independent new measurement -- flagged as such.
geometric_synthesis.function_dysfunction_anchor: Panjabi 1992 (PMID 1490034) 3-subsystem model (passive=vertebrae/discs/ligaments; active=muscles/tendons; neural=CNS+mechanoreceptor control) is the EXACT, verified, load-bearing anchor for the twin's own function<->dysfunction organizing axis: normal function = neural subsystem successfully directing the active subsystem to compensate for the passive subsystem's ~88N-only capacity; dysfunction (e.g., delayed TrA feedforward, C7) = a neural-subsystem timing failure that leaves the passive+active bracing under-prepared before load arrives.

honest_gaps: McGill & Norman 1987 (PMID 3443085), the foundational critique paper reassessing IAP's role in spinal compression, has NO abstract text retrievable via NCBI eutils this session (old Ergonomics record, matches the exact same 'no indexed abstract' pattern already documented for Pintar et al. 1992 in docs/MECHANISM_SPINE_LIGAMENTS.md) -- cited for its established role/title/DOI only, not for a specific extracted number.

Harman/Rosenstein/Frykman/Nigro 1989 belt-timing paper (PMID 2709981) reports IAP-timing effects (rises earlier with belt) but gives NO exact peak-mmHg or EMG number in its abstract -- the magnitude numbers used for C8 come from the 2 OTHER belt papers (McGill/Norman/Sharratt 1990, Lander et al. 1990), not this one.

The belt-reduces-erector-demand half of C8 is genuinely CONTESTED in the primary literature (1 paper for, 1 against) -- not resolved this session, reported as a live disagreement rather than smoothed over by picking the flattering result.

The IAP-extensor-moment crosscheck (C6) mixing Daggfeldt & Thorstensson's measured 10% fraction with this repo's own independently-derived N.m ceilings is an ILLUSTRATIVE, cross-population, cross-task, cross-pose estimate -- explicitly NOT a validated prediction; a real test would need the 10% fraction measured in the SAME pose/population/task this repo's OpenSim pipeline models.

Hodges & Richardson's exact millisecond-magnitude of the TrA delay (C7) is not extractable from either abstract fetched this session (both are qualitative: 'significantly delayed') -- the qualitative direction-independent-vs-direction-specific SIGNATURE is verified, the exact ms number is not, and neither abstract describes a dedicated general-reaction-time control condition, so the 'not a generic RT-slowing artifact' conclusion rests on the direction-independence PATTERN, not a directly measured RT-matched control.

The 3400N/6400N NIOSH action-limit/maximum-permissible-limit figures are widely cited (and already disclosed as such in this repo's own docs/MECHANISM_SPINE_FORCE.md) but the exact numbers are NOT stated in the Waters et al. 1993 abstract fetched this session (PMID 8339717) -- the abstract confirms the paper/equation exists and its biomechanical-criterion framing, not the specific N value.

All Crisco/Panjabi/Cholewicki/Gardner-Morse/Bergmark cohorts are SMALL (n=3 to n=10, one n=57 powerlifting cohort, one n=6 cadaveric) -- consistent with the era/field (1978-2003 spine biomechanics), not independently re-powered this session.

No new simulation was run on this repo's own MSK model this session -- this is a literature synthesis plus arithmetic cross-checks against ALREADY-PUBLISHED (this repo's own) OpenSim numbers, not a new build. A genuine next-step cell would ADD an IAP-generating force element (e.g., a pressurized-cavity constraint or an equivalent extensor-moment actuator, gated to the same TrA/multifidus/diaphragm/pelvic-floor co-contraction pattern) to the unified model and re-run Static Optimization -- not attempted here.
